title: Let’s Do Some Leaf-Peeping From Space - Nautilus
gist: A light piece that gathers NASA satellite images of autumn foliage. It notes that Earth's roughly 23-degree axial tilt drives seasonal change, and that tundra plants in Nunavut change color before the rest of the continent. The caption says the Nunavut image came from Landsat 9 in 2006, which looks like an internal date or satellite error.

insights.claim: NASA satellites observe Earth year-round and capture seasonal changes in vegetation, such as fall foliage, from orbit.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Continuous satellite imaging of vegetation underpins phenology data used in agriculture, forestry and climate analytics.
insights.quote: NASA satellites observe the Earth year-round

insights.claim: Tundra plants in Nunavut, such as willow, birch and blueberry shrubs, change color earlier than plants in other parts of North America because the region is close to the North Pole.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Latitude-driven timing of the seasons is a basic input to remote-sensing crop and forest models.
insights.quote: plants in this region, which include tundra flora like willow, birch, and blueberry shrubs, change colors earlier than other parts of the continent

insights.claim: Peak fall foliage depends on latitude and on weather conditions through the year, not only on the calendar.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Variable phenology affects seasonal tourism timing and vegetation-index signals.
insights.quote: peak leaf-peeping season depends on latitude and weather conditions throughout the year
